name: Serbian
family: Indo-European, Balto-Slavic, Slavic, South Slavic (western group, Serbo-Croatian)
variety: Standard Serbian (Neo-Štokavian norm, Ekavian as used in Belgrade and Novi Sad; the Ijekavian standard is used in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro). Written in Cyrillic and Latin script.
sources: Lehiste, Ilse & Ivić, Pavle (1986). Word and Sentence Prosody in Serbocroatian. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.
Lehiste, Ilse & Ivić, Pavle (1963). Accent in Serbocroatian: An Experimental Study. Ann Arbor: University of Michigan.
Inkelas, Sharon & Zec, Draga (1988). Serbo-Croatian pitch accent: the interaction of tone, stress, and intonation. Language 64, 227-248.
Zsiga, Elizabeth & Zec, Draga (2013). Contextual evidence for the representation of pitch accents in Standard Serbian. Language and Speech 56.
Smiljanić, Rajka (2004). Lexical, Pragmatic, and Positional Effects on Prosody in Two Dialects of Croatian and Serbian: An Acoustic Study. New York: Routledge.
Godjevac, Svetlana (2005). Transcribing Serbo-Croatian intonation. In Sun-Ah Jun (ed.), Prosodic Typology: The Phonology of Intonation and Phrasing. Oxford University Press.
Petrović, Dragoljub & Gudurić, Snežana (2010). Fonologija srpskoga jezika. Beograd: Institut za srpski jezik SANU.
Browne, Wayles (1993). Serbo-Croat. In B. Comrie & G. G. Corbett (eds.), The Slavonic Languages. London: Routledge.
contrasts: four word accents: short falling (kȕća), long falling (mȃjka), short rising (vòda), long rising (rúka)
vowel length under the accent and in syllables after the accent (post-accentual length: jùnāk, genitive plural žénā)
postalveolar /t͡ʃ d͡ʒ/ (č, dž) versus alveolo-palatal /t͡ɕ d͡ʑ/ (ć, đ), kept apart by speakers in Serbia
syllabic /r̩/, short or long, as a syllable nucleus that can carry the accent (krv, prst, srpski)
voiced versus voiceless obstruents, kept word-finally (grad [ɡraːd])
allophony: Ekavian: the reflex of jat is /e/ or /eː/ (mleko, lep, dete); Ijekavian Serbian has ije, je as in Croatian and Bosnian
no final devoicing; obstruent clusters take the voicing of their last member, mostly shown in the spelling (vrabac, vrapca), also between a proclitic and its host (od kuće [ot kut͡ɕe])
/ʋ/ is a weak labiodental approximant and neither causes nor undergoes voicing assimilation
/x/ is weak: a velar fricative that is [h]-like or dropped in colloquial speech
/n/ is [ŋ] before velars; /m/ is [ɱ] before /f ʋ/
/t d/ are dental; /r/ is an alveolar trill or tap; /l/ is slightly velarised
vowels keep their quality in unstressed syllables; short vowels, especially mid ones, are more open than long ones
post-accentual long vowels are shortened or lost by many Belgrade speakers, most of all in final open syllables
syllable_structure: (C)(C)(C)V(C)(C), with syllabic r as a possible nucleus
phonotactics: falling accents occur only on the first syllable of a word, rising accents on any syllable except the last; monosyllables have only falling accents
long vowels occur in the accented syllable and after it, never before it
proclitics can take over the accent of a word with a falling accent (u grad: ȕ grād)
coda clusters are few (st, zd, št, žd and sonorant plus obstruent)

stress.type: free (lexical) pitch accent, restricted by position
stress.rule: The accented syllable is lexical; it is never the last syllable of a polysyllabic word, and falling accents are limited to the first syllable. Ordinary spelling does not mark accent or length.
stress.cues: pitch pattern over the accented and the following syllable, duration, and intensity; vowel quality does not change

rhythm.notes: Often described as syllable-timed with added phonemic length; the class label is an impression from the descriptive literature.

length.notes: Long accented vowels are about one and a half times as long as short accented ones (Lehiste & Ivić 1986); post-accentual long vowels are shorter than accented long vowels.

intonation.declarative: each accented word carries its lexical accent shape; successive peaks are downstepped and the phrase ends low
intonation.yes_no_question: questions with da li or li end low like statements, with the verb or the focus high; questions marked by intonation alone have a low accented syllable on the focused word and a high peak on the next syllable whatever the lexical accent (Lehiste & Ivić's reverse pattern)
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word, then falling
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: falling accents: peak at the start of the accented syllable, low afterwards; rising accents: low to rising pitch on the accented syllable with the peak on the following syllable
intonation.notes: Belgrade and Novi Sad speakers keep the tonal contrast (Smiljanić 2004; Zsiga & Zec 2013).

inventory.name: short falling (kratkosilazni), marked ȁ
inventory.description: short accented vowel with the pitch peak at its beginning and a fall; the following syllable is low. Only on first syllables and monosyllables

inventory.name: long falling (dugosilazni), marked ȃ
inventory.description: long accented vowel with an early peak and a fall through the vowel; the following syllable is low. Only on first syllables and monosyllables

inventory.name: short rising (kratkouzlazni), marked à
inventory.description: short accented vowel with level or slightly rising pitch; the following syllable is as high or higher and carries the fall. Never on the last syllable

inventory.name: long rising (dugouzlazni), marked á
inventory.description: long accented vowel with pitch rising through the vowel; the following syllable starts high and then falls. Never on the last syllable

sandhi: a proclitic before a word with a falling accent can take over the accent (u grad: ȕ grād; ne znam: nè znām)
in intonation questions the lexical accent shapes are replaced by one low-high pattern on the focused word
tone.neutral_tone: syllables before the accent are mid; syllables after a falling accent are low; the first syllable after a rising accent is high and the rest are low
tone.notes: Chao numerals are a schematic rendering of the descriptions in Lehiste & Ivić (1986) and Inkelas & Zec (1988), not measured values. In tonal analyses a rising accent is a high tone on the syllable after the stressed one, a falling accent a high tone on the stressed (first) syllable itself.

problems: No pitch accent: the four accents are not distinguished and there are no tone phonemes. Accent marks in the text are ignored, except that acute-marked vowels are read as long.
No vowel length apart from a handful of words, so accented and post-accentual length are missing.
Stress is always on the first syllable. That is right for falling accents but wrong for words with a rising accent on a later syllable (lepòta, telèvīzija, interesàntan).

Syllabic r between consonants is a plain consonant (phoneme R2) and not a syllable nucleus: krv, prst, trg, smrt come out with no stressed syllable, and prvi, srpski, crkva, brzo are stressed on the last vowel.
Unstressed /a i u/ are replaced by reduced qualities ([ɐ], [ɪ], [ʊ]); the standard has no vowel reduction.
The letter e is open-mid [ɛ] but close [e] after j, which has no basis in the language.
Only the default eSpeak tunes are used; wh-questions get the same fall-rise as yes-no questions.
good: own phoneme table (inherits hr) with dental t, d, a trilled r and separate recordings for the č and ć, š and ž series, so č and ć, dž and đ are kept apart
regressive voicing assimilation, also between words (od kuće [ot])
lj and nj as single palatals [ʎ ɲ]
Cyrillic and Latin input both work; Ekavian or Ijekavian follows the spelling

notes: The rule and list files are shared with Croatian and Bosnian (sr_rules is identical to hr_rules; conditional entries ?2 and ?4 change names of symbols and numbers). No formant, VOT or rhythm-metric values are given because I cannot quote published figures with confidence.
